questions.question: According to the lesson's strategy, where is the main idea of a passage usually found?
options: Only in the middle paragraph
Strongly stated or implied in the first or last paragraph
Never explicitly stated anywhere
Only in the passage title
questions.rationale: The main idea is usually stated or strongly implied in the first or last paragraph, while other content supports it.

questions.question: When answering comprehension questions, your answer should be based on:
options: Your own outside knowledge of the topic
Only what the passage itself states
General assumptions about the subject
The most commonly known fact about the topic
questions.rationale: Even if you know more about the topic, your answer must be based only on what the passage says — comprehension tests reading skill, not general knowledge.

questions.question: Why should you be cautious of options containing words like 'always', 'never', or 'all'?
options: They are always the correct answer
They are frequently incorrect unless the passage uses equally absolute language
They should never appear in any passage
They only appear in inference questions
questions.rationale: Absolute words like 'always', 'never', 'all', or 'only' are frequently incorrect choices, since passages are usually more nuanced than that.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'False' answer and a 'Not Given' answer in True/False/Not Given questions?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
'Not Given' means the passage denies it; 'False' means it's simply absent
'False' means the passage denies it; 'Not Given' means it's simply absent from the passage
Both terms are used interchangeably in all exams
questions.rationale: The lesson stresses not to confuse 'not mentioned' (Not Given) with 'false' (directly contradicted by the passage) — they are different answers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of skimming on your first read of a passage?
options: To memorise every detail for later recall
To grasp the overall theme and structure without stopping at every unfamiliar word
To translate the passage word-for-word
To underline every absolute word you find
questions.rationale: The 'skim first, then scan' strategy says the first quick read captures overall theme and structure; detailed keyword scanning happens on a second pass.

questions.question: Under the elimination technique, which kind of MCQ option should you remove even if it sounds reasonable?
options: An option directly quoted from the passage
An option that is true in general but not stated in the passage
An option written in simple vocabulary
The longest option available
questions.rationale: Eliminate options that contradict the passage, options that are true in general but not stated in the passage, and options that are only partially correct.

questions.question: For a Central Idea / Title question, what approach does the lesson recommend?
options: Choose the option covering one smallest detail precisely
Look at the first and last paragraph and avoid options that cover only one small detail
Pick whichever option has the most words
Answer from the question's wording alone
questions.rationale: Central idea questions ask what the passage is mainly about — check the first and last paragraphs and reject options that capture just a supporting detail.

questions.question: How should you approach a Tone / Attitude question?
options: Look at adjectives, word choice, and any qualifying statements the author makes
Count how many facts appear in the passage
Check only the passage's title
Assume the tone is always objective
questions.rationale: Tone questions ask how the author feels about the subject — clues lie in the author's adjectives, word choice, and qualifying statements.

questions.question: For a Vocabulary-in-Context question, what does the lesson advise?
options: Recall the dictionary definition you know best
Re-read the sentence the word appears in and ignore its other possible dictionary meanings
Replace the word with any synonym you prefer
Skip such questions — context never clarifies meaning
questions.rationale: Vocabulary-in-context asks what the word means *here* — re-read the sentence where it appears rather than relying on its other dictionary senses.

questions.question: If time is limited, what does the lesson suggest for speed and accuracy?
options: Read only the final paragraph
Read the questions first so you know what to look for while reading the passage
Guess quickly on all factual-detail items
Read the passage aloud twice
questions.rationale: When time is short, read the questions first — then you scan the passage with specific keywords already in mind.

questions.question: In the solved passage 'Reading is to the mind what exercise is to the body', what does a love of reading give a person during hard times?
options: Wealth that grows over time
A companion that will never desert him in trouble
Improved physical strength
New career opportunities
questions.rationale: The passage says reading 'furnishes him with a companion that will never desert him in trouble', comparing reading to exercise that preserves bodily health.
